narrative:
Your law school application was denied because a predictive model assessed your likelihood of failing the bar exam on the first attempt at 76.6%. That is a high risk, and the admissions committee used that risk as a central signal in their decision. The model did not consider your gender or race; it focused on academic indicators from your school record and entrance exam.

The single most influential factor in this prediction was your class standing in your third year. You were in the first decile, meaning the bottom 10% of your class, while accepted applicants typically sit near the sixth decile. This was the strongest push toward a predicted failure. Your first-year class standing also worked against you: you were in the second decile, again far below the average accepted student. These two rankings alone created a consistent pattern of academic struggle that the model interpreted as preparation weakness.

Interestingly, your LSAT score was the only factor among the top three that pointed in the opposite direction—toward passing. Even though your score of 29.5 is below the average of 37.18 for accepted students, the model treated it as a slight relative strength, perhaps because it was not as far off as your class ranks. However, that positive influence was small compared to the negative impact of your low decile positions, so it could not overcome the overall risk.

To improve your chances, focus on transcript repair: retake key courses, aim for near-top grades, and consider a post-baccalaureate program to demonstrate a stronger academic trajectory. Raising your LSAT to at least the mid-30s would also strengthen your next application.
